newsitem.title: UK: Vote for UK Labour was vote for Euro-change -Blair.
newsitem.headline: Vote for UK Labour was vote for Euro-change -Blair.

text.p: The European Union must urgently change its ways to respond to the concerns of ordinary citizens, British Prime Minister Tony Blair said on Wednesday.

In an article for the Swedish paper Dagens Nyheter written for his visit on Thursday to the European Social Democratic Parties' Congress in the Swedish city of Malmo, Blair said his Labour party's landslide election victory last month was a mandate to play a constructive role in Europe. But it was not a vote for the status quo.
"It would be a great mistake to believe that the result on May 1 was a vote of confidence in the way the European Union currently operates. It was in fact a call for change," he said.
He said people in Sweden, as in Britain, felt remote from the decision-making process at EU headquarters in Brussels.
"They feel that the priorities of Europe's political and bureaucratic elites are too often out of step with the issues they face in their daily lives.

"That is why new Labour stood and was elected on a programme to reform the institutions and policies of the European Union, to make them more relevant to the needs and aspirations of our people," the Labour leader said.
Blair said it was fashionable to portray the EU's single currency as the key challenge facing Europe. He agreed the issue was vital, with tremendous repercussions if it was fumbled.
"But we face another immediate challenge. That is making the Union mean something to its citizens, whether they live in Malmo or Manchester, Munich or Milan," he said.

Blair listed five priorities that he said should help bring the EU closer to its citizens -- completion of the single market, enlargement of the 15-member bloc, farm reform, true foreign policy cooperation and a crusade against unemployment.

Earlier on Wednesday, Britain's finance minister, Gordon Brown, launched an initiative to cut unemployment across Europe by proposing EU-wide measures to make people more employable and to lower the barriers to job creation.
Blair said Britain wanted an employment chapter in the new treaty revising the EU's rules and institutions, which is due to be completed at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17.
But he issued a warning against taking any action to create jobs that could damage Europe's global competitiveness.
"The risk that the employment chapter might backfire, putting in jeopardy more jobs than it creates, is not one that I am prepared to take," Blair wrote.
He said Sweden and Britain also agreed that the EU needed to play a greater role in environmental protection and to open up its often arcane workings to greater public scrutiny.

"Is it any wonder that people are suspicious of the Union when the Council of Ministers continues to make laws in secret?" Blair asked, saying he would back proposals at Amsterdam for EU institutions to conduct their business more openly.
